segments.text: At 40, everyone's arms get too short. <break time="350ms"/> Close-up text blurs, so the phone goes further and further away.

826 million people can't see well up close, because their eyes aren't corrected. <break time="250ms"/> Reading glasses cost about two dollars, and in randomised trials, they raised productivity by 22%, and income by a third.
The hard part is choosing the strength. <break time="200ms"/> Shop charts only work at exactly the right distance, at the right print size, and only if you can read.
Small Print turns your phone's camera into a ruler. <break time="200ms"/> It measures how far your eyes are from the screen, right on the device. First, hold the phone where you like to read.
Then just swipe the way the E points. No reading needed.
The E is redrawn about 30 times a second, so it always looks the same size to your eye, while the test finds the closest distance where you still see sharply.
Out comes a starting strength for ready-made reading glasses.
Then check a pair in the shop. <break time="200ms"/> With the glasses on, the app measures where you see sharply, and checks that your reading distance sits in the middle.

Video never leaves the phone, and there are no AI guesses about your eyes. <break time="250ms"/> It's built on AWS, with CloudFront, Lambda, DynamoDB and Polly, for about 60 cents per 1,000 screenings.
Small Print. <break time="300ms"/> Everyone deserves to read the small print.
